clue.text: Stone area very quiet in Staffs, for one

indicators.note: the area and very-quiet letters are placed inside the county word

parts.note: Staffs (Staffordshire) is an example of an English county, a shire
PP, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very quiet

explanation.surface: Someone describes a gemstone found in a quiet corner of Staffordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffs is short for Staffordshire, an English county; 'for one' marks it as an example of a SHIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapphire is a precious gemstone, usually blue, so it is an example of a stone.

clue.text: Take action to pen secret number on back

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the action word encloses the number

parts.note: to sue is to take legal action
a PIN is a secret personal identification number

explanation.surface: Someone acts to write down a hidden code on the reverse of a card.
explanation.definitionFit: Supine means lying face upward, that is lying on one's back.

clue.text: Display fourth chunk of text at bottom of page

parts.note: a para is a paragraph, a chunk of text
D is the fourth letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: the bottom of a down word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A printer shows the fourth paragraph at the foot of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: A parade is a public procession or show, so a display.

clue.text: Splendid large piece —— why, say, fish?

parts.note: a hunk is a large piece

indicators.note: say means the word is spoken and gives the letter that sounds like it

parts.note: the word why sounds like the letter Y
a dory is a sea fish, the John Dory

explanation.surface: Someone admires a big chunk of something and asks why it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunky-dory is informal for fine or excellent, so it means splendid.

clue.text: Two Bears, by English poet

parts.note: Rupert Bear is a cartoon bear from a long-running British comic strip
to brook is to bear or tolerate

explanation.surface: A pair of bears stand beside an English poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two Bears' gives two pieces: Rupert, the British children's cartoon bear, and BROOK, the verb to bear. Rupert Brooke was the English First World War poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Rupert Brooke was an English poet best known for his war sonnets, so he is an example of a poet.

clue.text: Seaman left by a bare rock

parts.note: a scar is a steep bare rocky outcrop on a hillside

explanation.surface: A sailor is abandoned beside a naked crag.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar is an Indian or Southeast Asian sailor, historically crewing European ships, so a type of seaman.

clue.text: A number of people coming to watch a gem

parts.words: number of people coming to watch
parts.note: the gate is the number of spectators attending a match

explanation.surface: A crowd turns up to admire a jewel.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a banded semiprecious stone, so it is a gem.

clue.text: Place oil wrongly in something powered by steam

indicators.note: wrongly suggests the letters are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone puts oil in the wrong place in a steam engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A calliope is a steam organ, a keyboard instrument whose whistles are blown by steam.

clue.text: Agree end to torture for traitor

indicators.note: to torture is to twist, so these letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A turncoat consents to have the torture stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end to torture' reads as stopping torture, but 'to torture' is the anagram signal on AGREE and END.
explanation.definitionFit: A renegade is one who deserts a cause or side, which makes him a traitor.

clue.text: Veg not quite trim, needing little cuts

indicators.note: not quite the full word: its final letter is lopped off

parts.note: to pare is to trim
snips are small cuts made with scissors

explanation.surface: A cook's vegetables are under-trimmed and need a few more small cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsnips are root vegetables, and veg is the informal short form for vegetables.

clue.text: Killed in fine bog in Ireland

parts.note: F is the pencil abbreviation for fine
the Bog of Allen is a large peat bog in central Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone dies in a pleasant Irish marsh.
explanation.definitionFit: The fallen are those killed in battle, so fallen is used as a synonym for killed.

clue.text: Very helpful, doing without singers

definitions.meaning: being ... in something means playing a key, helpful part in it
music played only by instruments with no vocals

explanation.definitionFit: Instrumental means both crucially helpful and, of music, performed without voices.

clue.text: No parent lets a daughter drop childish character

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the parent word drops the named letters from inside it
the parent word drops the named letters from inside it

parts.note: daddy is a parent, a father

explanation.surface: A father refuses to let his little girl fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lets ... drop' removes A and D from DADDY, leaving DDY. Noddy is the little wooden boy in Enid Blyton's children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Noddy is a character from British children's books, so he is a childish character in the sense of one for children.

clue.text: Recall maintaining purpose in translation

indicators.note: maintaining means holding, so the recall word holds the purpose word inside it

parts.note: to re-ring is to call again on the phone, to recall
an end is an aim or purpose

explanation.surface: Someone remembering, while keeping their goal in view, works on a translation.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendering is a version or interpretation of a text in another language, which is a translation.

clue.text: Primed to explode, baby torpedo goes off with power

indicators.note: goes off suggests something going wrong, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A small torpedo detonates with force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes off' scrambles BABY, TORPEDO and P (power) together; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something booby-trapped is rigged with a hidden device ready to detonate, so it is primed to explode.

clue.text: Inventor's boat, approaching island, impaled by top of reef

indicators.note: the boat comes just before the island word in the answer

parts.note: Noah's ark is a boat

indicators.note: impaled means pierced, so a letter is stuck inside the island word

parts.note: the Isle of Wight is an island off southern England

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An inventor's boat nears an island and is pierced by a jagged reef.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Arkwright invented the water frame for spinning cotton; the 's is a link meaning has.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Arkwright devised the spinning frame in the Industrial Revolution, so he is an example of an inventor.

clue.text: Like a priest, has gone off wildly enthusiastic

indicators.note: gone off means gone bad or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: manic means frenzied or wildly excited

explanation.surface: A priest has gone away in a frenzy of excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: Shamanic describes a shaman, a tribal priest and healer, so it means like a priest.

clue.text: Son getting sack in a sloppy affair

parts.note: to sack a town is to pillage it

explanation.surface: A son is fired in a messy business.
explanation.definitionFit: A spillage is an accidental spill, a messy, sloppy occurrence.

clue.text: Carefree? I'm surprised: brave about recurrence of old pain

parts.note: ha is an exclamation of surprise

indicators.note: the brave word goes about, around, the other pieces

parts.note: plucky means brave

indicators.note: recurrence suggests running back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: gyp is British slang for pain, as in giving someone gyp

explanation.surface: Someone expresses surprise that a person cheerfully bears an old ache returning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recurrence of' reverses the old-pain letters to give PYGO. Gyp is British informal for pain, as in 'my knee is giving me gyp'.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy-go-lucky describes someone cheerfully unconcerned about the future, which is carefree.

clue.text: Sort of music cut out of good books

indicators.note: the cut word lies outside the books letters

parts.note: mown means cut, as of grass
OT, the Old Testament, is a set of books of the Good Book

explanation.surface: Someone falls out of favour over a kind of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut out of good books' looks like falling from favour; really MOWN goes outside OT.
explanation.definitionFit: Motown is a style of soul music named after the Detroit record label, so it is a sort of music.

clue.text: Money has to go round: they may well be laughing

indicators.note: the has word goes round the money word

parts.note: the yen is Japan's currency, money

explanation.surface: Funds must circulate, and those holding them may be smiling.
explanation.walkthrough: The laughing hyena is so called for its cackling call.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyenas are known as laughing animals for their cackling cry, so they may be laughing.

clue.text: Numbers of Romans not great about a British port

parts.note: M, I and L are Roman numerals

indicators.note: the small word goes about, around, the other letters

parts.note: wee means small, not great
UK is the United Kingdom, standing for British

explanation.surface: Something about Roman numbers being underwhelming around a British harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Milwaukee in Wisconsin is a port on Lake Michigan; 'British' misleads as part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Milwaukee is a major lake port on Lake Michigan, so it is an example of a port.

clue.text: Holder of world title initially admitted to expression of regret

indicators.note: the initial letter is let into the regret word

parts.note: alas is an exclamation of regret

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A world champion first admits regret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holder of world title' looks like a champion, but 'title initially' is the wordplay. In myth the Titan Atlas held up the world.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan Atlas bore the heavens on his shoulders, often shown holding up the globe.

clue.text: Without cramping low in your back

indicators.note: back means the combined letters are read backwards
the low word goes inside the your abbreviation

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: Someone stretches out comfortably while their back is low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the whole assembly, giving ROOMY from YMOOR; 'low' is the cow's verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Roomy means spacious, with plenty of space, so without cramping describes it.

clue.text: Not quite new? Ancient

parts.note: early can mean belonging to a remote past, ancient

explanation.surface: Something is not quite new but rather old.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly means almost, and something almost done is not quite done.

clue.text: Cut round label and handle

indicators.note: the cut word goes round the label word

parts.note: shorn means cut, as of hair or fleece
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: Someone trims around a label and a grip.
explanation.definitionFit: Staghorn, deer antler, is a traditional material for knife handles, so a staghorn is a kind of handle.

clue.text: Stop collecting runs, stuck here?

indicators.note: the stop word collects the runs letter inside it

parts.note: cease means stop
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A batsman stops scoring runs and is stuck at the batting line.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the crease is the line where the batsman stands; a batsman not scoring is stuck there.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman who is not scoring stays stuck at the crease, the line marked where he bats.

clue.text: Philosopher's American parking space?

parts.note: a lot is a plot or space of ground
being American means being in the US

explanation.surface: A philosopher owns a parking spot in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Plotinus was a Greek-speaking Neoplatonist philosopher of the third century.
explanation.definitionFit: Plotinus was a third-century Neoplatonist thinker, so he is an example of a philosopher.
